findings.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:123 — P1, confidence 100: `granted.add(groupResource.getId());` supplies the authorization-resource primary key rather than the group id stored as the resource name, so group-member-scoped user search and count queries filter memberships with non-group IDs and return no authorized users.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:121 — P2, confidence 100: `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, groupResource -> { if (hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW_MEMBERS, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERS)) { ... } });` performs a resource lookup and full authorization evaluation for every group resource on each restricted user search/count, so a tenant with many groups turns one admin request into an unbounded N-query/evaluation fan-out.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:70 — P1, confidence 100: `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);` makes an all-groups `view` grant satisfy `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup`'s `requireManage()`, so a view-only administrator can create or move groups while the added tests never assert that VIEW is non-mutating.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:123 — P1 (confidence 100): `granted.add(groupResource.getId())` records the authorization resource ID instead of the group-model ID expected by `UserModel.GROUPS`, so a group-scoped `view-members` or `manage-members` grant makes user-search and brute-force endpoints return 200 while silently omitting every permitted group member.

goldens.comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:121 — P2, confidence 100: `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, groupResource -> { if (hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW_MEMBERS, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERS)) { ... } });` performs a resource lookup and full authorization evaluation for every group resource on each restricted user search/count, so a tenant with many groups turns one admin request into an unbounded N-query/evaluation fan-out.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() in GroupPermissionsV2.java iterates over all group resources via resourceStore.findByType() and calls hasPermission() for each one, which performs authorization evaluation. This is a real performance concern for realms with many groups. However, this is not a bug (the code is functionally correct) but rather a scalability/architecture concern. The diff shows this is new code in GroupPermissionsV2.java that replaces the V1 implementation which had similar iteration patterns. The concern is valid and grounded in the actual diff code at lines 113-123.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:70 — P1, confidence 100: `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);` makes an all-groups `view` grant satisfy `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup`'s `requireManage()`, so a view-only administrator can create or move groups while the added tests never assert that VIEW is non-mutating.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:123 — P1 (confidence 100): `granted.add(groupResource.getId())` records the authorization resource ID instead of the group-model ID expected by `UserModel.GROUPS`, so a group-scoped `view-members` or `manage-members` grant makes user-search and brute-force endpoints return 200 while silently omitting every permitted group member.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.java:123, the code does `granted.add(groupResource.getId())`. The `groupResource` is obtained from `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` which returns authorization Resource objects. The Resource's `getId()` returns the authorization resource ID, not the group model ID. However, looking at AdminPermissionsSchema.java, when creating resources via `getOrCreateResource`, for groups it calls `resolveGroup` which returns `group.getId()` (the group model ID), and this is used as the resource name. Looking at line 119 in GroupPermissionsV2.java, it iterates over resources and adds `groupResource.getId()` - but the authorization Resource ID is different from the group ID. The resource is created with the group ID as its name (not its ID). This means `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` returns authorization resource IDs instead of group model IDs, which would cause the user search filtering to fail silently since `UserModel.GROUPS` expects group model IDs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:74 — `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)) { manager.register(...) }` changes provider-listener registration lifecycle instead of adding the Groups resource type and scopes, expanding the stated authorization-schema task into unrelated event-wiring behavior (P2, confidence 75).

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims this change is unrelated to the stated task, but the diff shows this is a valid optimization - moving the feature flag check outside the event listener registration to avoid registering a listener that would do nothing when the feature is disabled. This is a reasonable refactoring that improves efficiency. The change doesn't 'expand into unrelated event-wiring behavior' - it simply restructures existing code to check the feature flag once at registration time rather than on every event. This is not a bug, not an important non-bug issue, but rather a mischaracterization of a valid code improvement.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:267 — P1, confidence 100: `createGroupPermission(myGroup, Set.of(VIEW), policy);` is followed only by listing assertions, so the suite passes when the new `GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` treats a global `VIEW` grant as `MANAGE` and lets a view-only administrator create groups.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() treats a global VIEW grant as MANAGE. Looking at the diff, GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() checks for AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS role OR hasPermission with AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW and MANAGE scopes. However, the test at line 267 creates a VIEW permission for a specific group (myGroup), not a global permission. The test then verifies that myadmin can only view myGroup (hasSize(1)), not that they can manage/create groups. The subsequent createAllGroupsPermission with VIEW scope is separate. The canManage() method requires MANAGE scope for actual management operations - the VIEW scope in hasPermission is for canView() methods. The finding misreads the code logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:293 — P2, confidence 100: `createAllUserPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE, policy, Set.of(MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP));` and `createGroupPermission(topGroup, Set.of(MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP), policy);` are granted together before the only success assertion, so the test passes if either half of the required user-and-group authorization check is silently omitted and an administrator changes membership with only one scope.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test design issue in the new test file. Looking at the test `testManageGroupMembership()` around line 280-293, both `createAllUserPermission(policy, Set.of(MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP))` and `createGroupPermission(topGroup, Set.of(MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP), policy)` are granted before calling `joinGroup()`. The test only verifies the happy path where both permissions are present. It doesn't verify that the operation fails when only one permission is granted (either user permission without group permission, or vice versa). This is a legitimate test coverage gap - the test should verify that BOTH permissions are required, not just that having both works. However, this is a test quality issue, not a bug in the production code.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points out a valid test coverage gap. Looking at the diff, `UserPermissionsV2.canMapRoles` now has group-fallback logic (`canManageByGroup(user)`) at line 84-85, but the test `testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers` only tests user update via `MANAGE_MEMBERS` permission, not role mapping. The test calls `update()` which exercises `canManage()`, not `canMapRoles()`. There's no test in the diff that specifically verifies the `canMapRoles` method's new group-fallback behavior. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added logic, though the claim about 'reject role mapping' is speculative since the fallback should actually allow it.
